**A Gaussian process specifies how function values at different inputs vary together.** The kernel says which inputs should have correlated outputs. Conditioning that joint Gaussian distribution on observed data yields a predictive mean and variance at a new input. [1](https://gaussianprocess.org/gpml/)

Near well-observed points, uncertainty often falls under a suitable kernel; far from observations, it reflects the prior more strongly. The formulas below combine kernel similarities with observed residuals using a linear solve.

**Bayesian optimization uses both prediction and uncertainty.** Expected improvement asks how much a candidate might beat the current best, balancing a promising mean with uncertainty that could reveal a better region. A point with lower predicted value can still be worth evaluating if uncertainty is substantial.

Dense GP fitting costs cubic time in observation count and quadratic storage, so it is best suited to relatively small expensive-evaluation settings unless approximated. Use Cholesky solves, handle zero predictive variance in acquisition calculations, and inspect kernel assumptions. High-dimensional, discontinuous, or constrained problems may favor other surrogates. A GP uncertainty estimate is only as credible as its modeling assumptions and data.

**Technical details and references.**

A GP assigns jointly Gaussian values to every finite set of input locations with mean $m$ and covariance kernel $k$. With Gaussian observation noise $\sigma^2$, let $K_y=K(X,X)+\sigma^2I$. The posterior mean at $x_*$ is $m_*+k_*^TK_y^{-1}(y-m)$ and variance is $k_{**}-k_*^TK_y^{-1}k_*$. [1](https://gaussianprocess.org/gpml/)

Use Cholesky solves, not an explicit inverse; dense factorization costs $O(N^3)$ time and $O(N^2)$ storage. For maximization, expected improvement is $(\mu-f_{best}-\xi)\Phi(z)+\sigma\phi(z)$ with $z=(\mu-f_{best}-\xi)/\sigma$, using the zero-variance limit when needed. GPs are a strong Bayesian-optimization baseline for expensive, modest-dimensional smooth problems, not universally the gold standard. Kernel mismatch, noise, constraints, and large/high-dimensional datasets motivate alternative surrogates or approximations.
